stages.name: persist
stages.notes: Research brief updated after recording the outcome and decision

briefs.researchQuestion: Libraries regularly ship 'minor' or 'patch' updates that break the code of everyone using them, even though those updates are installed automatically on the promise of being safe. Could a small open-source tool catch these breaks before a release is published?
briefs.whyItMatters: Every JavaScript project depends on dozens to hundreds of packages and trusts version numbers to signal risk. When a minor release breaks that trust, users lose time pinning versions and debugging, and maintainers lose credibility. Rust has a widely adopted tool for this; JavaScript has no established equivalent.
subQuestions: How often do popular npm packages ship breaking changes in minor or patch releases?
What kinds of breaks are they: type changes, behaviour changes, or metadata changes?
What do existing and emerging tools catch, and what do they miss?
Is there a small, buildable tool that catches a meaningful share with little noise?

findings.statement: Breaking minor and patch releases cost users real time. Reports describe whole codebases breaking after a React minor update, release pipelines broken for a weekend, and maintainers forced to pin versions. Microsoft built API Extractor partly because users 'keep reporting that their code won't compile after a supposedly minor update'.
findings.strength: Moderate. Several independent reports plus Microsoft's own stated motivation. Individual cases, not a measured rate.

findings.statement: The tool model works elsewhere: Rust's cargo-semver-checks (about 1,700 stars, with a GitHub Action) checks releases for semver violations, though it documents breaks it can't catch.
findings.strength: Strong as evidence that a tool exists and is adopted in Rust. It doesn't show JS maintainers would adopt one.

findings.statement: The TypeScript type-surface checker niche is filling up: Clerk's break-check (company-backed), ts-semver-checks and semver-check all appeared in 2026, alongside Microsoft's API Extractor.
findings.strength: Strong for existence. All are very new, with little adoption yet.

findings.statement: Type checkers miss many real breaks. None of the four complaints examined was a type change: they were behaviour changes (React, floating-ui, node-abort-controller) and a metadata change (polished raised its required Node version in a minor release).
findings.strength: Weak to moderate. A small sample, but it points to a clear gap: the install and import contract in package metadata.

findings.statement: Metadata-level contract breaks are common: by the linter's rules, 20% of 400 popular npm packages shipped at least one in a minor or patch release over two years. But as specified the rules are too noisy: only 8 of 20 audited flags were genuine breaks. Most of the rest were debatable engine-range changes dropping end-of-life Node versions.
findings.strength: Moderate. A pre-registered measurement plus a hand audit of 20 flags against criteria fixed beforehand (one reviewer).

findings.statement: The structural rules are the useful core. Removed export paths, entry fields and CLI commands, and tightened peers, were genuine in 7 of 9 audited cases, but they fire for only about 10% of popular packages over two years. Many flags come from a few fast-moving projects (@tanstack, better-auth, @typescript-eslint).
findings.strength: Weak to moderate. Exploratory, post hoc, small n.

uncertainties: How often metadata-level breaks actually happen in popular packages (being measured).
Whether maintainers consider deliberate engine bumps in minor releases acceptable.
The four complaints were chosen by GitHub search ranking, not sampled randomly.

conclusion.belief: Accidental breaking releases are real, and a cheap metadata check can catch a share of them that type checkers miss: removed export paths, entry points and CLI commands, and tightened peers. But it's a modest benefit (about 1 in 10 popular packages over two years). As first specified, engine-range rules make it too noisy. The practical value is a small, precise rule set, best contributed as a 'compare with last release' mode to an existing packaging linter such as publint. That would be useful open-source work, but not a standalone product.
conclusion.confidenceReason: A pre-registered measurement over 12,240 release pairs plus an audited sample. Not high: the audit had one reviewer and 20 flags, and the narrowed rule set's precision comes from only 9 audited cases.
unknowns: The narrowed rule set's precision on a fresh sample
Whether publint's maintainers would want this feature
How often flagged breaks actually hurt users (issues filed after release)
conclusion.continueReason: One cheap step remains: validate the narrowed rule set on a fresh, independently drawn audit sample before proposing it upstream.

nextSteps.text: Validate the structural-only rule set on a fresh random sample of 20 flags not in the first audit (pre-registered: ≥ 70% genuine).
If it holds, prototype a 'compare with last release' check, and ask the owner whether VENTURE may propose it to the publint maintainers. That means contacting people, so it needs authorization.
